title: Why 90% of Traders Quit Before They Become Profitable: The Hidden Valley Between Losses and Long-Term Success
author: tickeron_community
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/xmqi40mu76zh1.jpeg

*The most difficult stage of trading isn't learning how to buy or sell. It's surviving the period when your knowledge is improving, but your account balance isn't.*

# Key Takeaways

* **The most dangerous phase in trading is the drawdown-to-breakeven period.** Traders begin with expectations of steady profits, experience unexpected losses, and often abandon their strategies before they have gathered enough evidence to determine whether those strategies work.
* **The image highlights the point where “90% of traders quit.”** This is a powerful illustration of trading psychology, but the 90% figure is not established by the chart and should not be treated as a verified statistical finding.
* **Trading progress is rarely linear.** Learning, risk management, emotional discipline, and strategy refinement can improve even while short-term trading results remain disappointing.
* **Tickeron's Financial Learning Models (FLMs)** can help traders evaluate market patterns, compare trading signals, and develop more systematic decision-making processes rather than relying exclusively on intuition.
* [**Tickeron's AI Robots**](https://tickeron.com/app/ai-robots/trending-robots/)**, AI Screener, and Ask AI** can support research, trade selection, and ongoing performance evaluation. These tools can reduce some analytical work, but they cannot eliminate market risk or guarantee profitability.
* **The goal is not simply to survive losses until profits arrive.** Successful traders must distinguish between normal statistical variation in a potentially profitable strategy and persistent losses caused by a strategy that has no demonstrated edge.

 

# 1. The Most Important Part of the Chart Is Where 90% of Traders Quit

Look carefully at the image.

Two lines tell very different stories.

The green line represents what most beginning traders expect: consistent progress, steady gains, and an account balance that rises almost immediately.

The orange line represents a more difficult learning journey.

Initially, there is little progress. Then losses appear. The account enters a drawdown. Confidence deteriorates.

Eventually, in the illustration, the orange line recovers, crosses breakeven, and begins accelerating upward.

https://i.redd.it/rboo3pa286zh1.png

But the most important part of the image isn't the final upward curve.

**It's the valley where the orange line reaches its lowest point.**

That is the point labeled:

**“The drawdown and breakeven phase where 90% quit.”**

The 90% figure is best understood as an illustrative warning, not a measured probability. Nevertheless, the behavioral problem it describes is real.

Many traders abandon their plans after experiencing losses, particularly when their expectations were unrealistic.

The paradox is that this may happen precisely when they have begun learning important lessons about risk, execution, and market behavior.

However, there is an equally important distinction: continuing to trade does not automatically lead to profitability.

The challenge is learning when persistence is justified—and when the strategy itself needs to change.

# 2. Why Beginners Expect Trading Profits to Grow in a Straight Line

Most beginners enter the market with a relatively simple assumption.

They believe that if they study technical indicators, identify promising stocks, and follow trading signals, their profits should gradually increase.

The expectation looks something like this:

**Month 1:** Learn the strategy.

**Month 2:** Start making small profits.

**Month 3:** Become more consistent.

**Month 6:** Increase position sizes.

**Month 12:** Generate meaningful trading income.

Unfortunately, financial markets do not reward effort in such a predictable sequence.

A trader can make a well-reasoned decision and still lose money.

A trader can also make a poor decision and earn a profit.

This creates a difficult learning environment because immediate financial outcomes do not always reveal the quality of the underlying decisions.

Consider a trading strategy with a hypothetical 45% win rate and an average winning trade twice the size of its average losing trade.

Such a strategy has positive theoretical expectancy before costs.

Yet it will still lose on 55% of individual trades.

Even a strategy with favorable mathematical expectancy can experience losing streaks and substantial drawdowns.

**A losing trade is not necessarily evidence of a bad strategy. But a long series of losses is not automatically evidence that success is just around the corner.**

Understanding this distinction is essential.

# 3. The Drawdown Phase: Where Confidence Begins to Collapse

The orange curve in the image moves below its starting point.

This represents a period when the trader's account is losing money despite continued effort.

Psychologically, this stage can be devastating.

The trader begins questioning everything.

Was the strategy wrong?

Were the indicators misleading?

Should I change the timeframe?

Should I switch from stocks to options?

Should I increase position sizes to recover losses?

These questions can produce a destructive cycle.

A trader loses money using one strategy, switches to another, experiences more losses, and then abandons that strategy as well.

Instead of developing expertise, the trader repeatedly starts over.

# The Strategy-Hopping Trap

Imagine a trader who begins with a moving-average crossover strategy.

After ten losing trades, the trader switches to RSI reversals.

When that strategy encounters a difficult market, the trader moves to breakout trading.

Next comes options trading, followed by leveraged ETFs.

After six months, the trader has experimented with five strategies but collected insufficient consistent data to evaluate any of them properly.

The problem may not be a lack of intelligence or effort.

It may be the absence of a structured process for determining whether a strategy has a statistical edge.

This is one reason the drawdown phase can become the point where traders give up.

# 4. The Breakeven Phase: The Most Frustrating Stage of Trading

The image also highlights the breakeven period.

This phase can be especially frustrating because the trader may be working harder and making better decisions without seeing meaningful account growth.

The trader might have improved in several areas:

* Entering trades with more discipline.
* Avoiding impulsive purchases.
* Using stop-loss orders consistently.
* Reducing unnecessary trading activity.
* Selecting setups more carefully.
* Recognizing unfavorable market conditions.

Yet the account balance may remain approximately unchanged.

Why?

Because improvements in trading behavior do not necessarily translate immediately into higher profits.

Market conditions can change, sample sizes can be small, and transaction costs can consume a meaningful portion of gross gains.

A breakeven period may indicate progress, but it can also indicate that the strategy lacks sufficient expectancy after costs.

The distinction requires measurement.

**The trader who learns to evaluate results objectively has a better foundation for improvement than the trader who relies on hope.**

 

# 5. What Actually Separates Traders Who Improve From Those Who Quit?

The difference is not simply patience.

It is the combination of patience, evidence, risk management, and adaptability.

# A. They Measure Their Strategies

Professional trading requires more than remembering winning trades.

Traders should track:

|**Performance metric**|**Why it matters**|
|:-|:-|
|Win rate|Percentage of profitable trades|
|Average gain|Typical profit from winning trades|
|Average loss|Typical loss from losing trades|
|Profit factor|Gross profits divided by gross losses|
|Maximum drawdown|Largest peak-to-trough account decline|
|Expectancy|Expected profit or loss per trade|
|Transaction costs|Commissions, spreads, and slippage|
|Performance by market regime|Whether results depend on particular conditions|

For example, a trader with a 40% win rate can still be profitable if average gains are sufficiently larger than average losses.

But a trader winning 70% of the time can lose money if occasional losses are disproportionately large.

The objective is not to maximize the percentage of winning trades.

It is to develop a repeatable process with positive expectancy after costs.

# B. They Control Position Sizes

One of the biggest reasons traders struggle to recover from drawdowns is excessive risk.

Consider the mathematics:

|**Account drawdown**|**Gain required to recover**|
|:-|:-|
|−10%|\+11.1%|
|−20%|\+25.0%|
|−30%|\+42.9%|
|−40%|\+66.7%|
|−50%|\+100.0%|

A trader who loses half an account must double the remaining capital merely to return to the original balance.

This is why protecting capital is more important than trying to recover losses quickly.

A common risk-management framework is to limit planned losses to a small percentage of account equity per trade, such as 0.5%–1%, although actual execution losses can exceed the planned amount.

# C. They Stop Confusing Activity With Progress

More trades do not necessarily produce more profits.

In fact, excessive trading can increase transaction costs, emotional stress, and exposure to poor-quality setups.

Sometimes the most valuable trading decision is to remain in cash.

A trader who avoids five unfavorable setups may be making more progress than one who executes five unnecessary trades.

 

# 6. How Tickeron's Financial Learning Models Can Help Traders Navigate the Difficult Phase

One of the challenges facing individual traders is the sheer volume of information required to evaluate the market.

A trader may need to monitor price trends, momentum, volatility, earnings announcements, market conditions, and risk simultaneously.

This is where artificial intelligence can provide analytical support.

Rather than relying entirely on manually interpreted indicators, traders can use FLM-based tools as an additional perspective on market behavior.

# FLMs and Strategy Development

A trader using a traditional technical strategy might begin with three indicators:

* The 200-period EMA to determine trend direction.
* The 20-period EMA to identify potential pullbacks.
* RSI to evaluate momentum.

An FLM-based signal can then provide another input for evaluating whether the setup deserves attention.

However, agreement between an FLM and traditional indicators does not guarantee a profitable trade.

The signals may also reflect overlapping market information.

The real question is whether FLM confirmation improves results over a sufficiently large out-of-sample test.

# 7. Why the Final Orange Curve Can Be Misleading

The image ends with a sharply accelerating orange curve.

It labels this stage the result of compounding and mastery.

This captures an important idea: consistent percentage returns can compound over time.

But the illustration also creates a potential misconception.

**There is no inevitable upward curve waiting for every trader who survives the drawdown phase.**

Some strategies never become profitable.

Others work temporarily and then deteriorate as market conditions change.

Even highly experienced traders experience drawdowns.

Compounding magnifies positive returns over time, but losses and volatility interrupt that process.

A more realistic understanding is that trading improvement can increase the probability of making better decisions, while profitability remains uncertain.

The appropriate goal is not to endure unlimited losses until success arrives.

It is to preserve enough capital and analytical flexibility to recognize whether the strategy is improving.

# 8. The Five Stages of Trading Development

The image can be interpreted as a journey through five distinct stages.

**Stage 1: Optimism**

The trader expects relatively quick profits and believes technical indicators will make market direction predictable.

**Stage 2: Reality**

Losing trades, market volatility, and unexpected news expose weaknesses in the original assumptions.

**Stage 3: The Quitting Zone**

Drawdowns and inconsistent results produce frustration. The trader may abandon the strategy, increase risk, or leave trading entirely.

**Stage 4: Evidence-Based Improvement**

The trader begins measuring performance, reducing unnecessary risks, and distinguishing between market noise and genuine strategy weaknesses.

**Stage 5: Sustainable Execution**

If a strategy demonstrates positive expectancy, the trader focuses on consistent implementation, controlling drawdowns, and adapting when market conditions change.

Not every trader reaches Stage 5, and reaching it does not guarantee continuously rising profits.

The critical transition is from trading based on expectations to trading based on evidence.

 

# 9. A Practical Plan for Traders Who Are Currently in the “90% Quit” Zone

For someone experiencing a difficult drawdown, the appropriate response is not automatically to continue trading.

A more disciplined process is to reassess the evidence.

**First, reduce risk.** Avoid increasing position sizes simply to recover previous losses.

**Second, review the trading journal.** Determine whether losses resulted from poor execution, an unfavorable market regime, or a strategy with negative expectancy.

**Third, test before scaling.** Use historical data and paper trading to evaluate revised rules without immediately risking additional capital.

**Fourth, separate process quality from financial outcomes.** A well-executed losing trade may be acceptable; a profitable trade taken outside the rules may still reflect poor discipline.

**Fifth, establish stopping conditions.** Define a maximum acceptable drawdown and clear criteria for suspending or abandoning a strategy.

The goal is to make persistence conditional on evidence—not emotion.

# 10. Final Thoughts: The Point Where Traders Quit Can Also Be the Point Where They Learn the Most

The most powerful message in the image is not the promise of exponential profits.

It is the contrast between expectations and reality.

Most beginners imagine that trading success should begin immediately and progress steadily.

Real markets are uncertain. Trading strategies experience losing streaks. Psychological pressure can cause otherwise capable people to abandon discipline.

The drawdown-to-breakeven phase is particularly difficult because progress may be invisible in the account balance.

Yet this is also where traders can develop essential skills: risk management, patience, statistical thinking, and objective performance evaluation.

Tickeron's Financial Learning Models, [AI Robots](https://tickeron.com/app/ai-robots/trending-robots/), AI Screener, and Ask AI can support this learning process by providing additional analytical tools and structured signals.

They do not replace the need for independent testing and sound risk management.

**The lesson is not “Never quit.”**

**The lesson is: Don't quit simply because progress is slower than expected—and don't continue risking money simply because you believe success must eventually come.**

A sustainable trading process requires the wisdom to know the difference.

comments.body: I think the real challenge is telling the difference between normal drawdowns and a strategy that simply has no edge. Staying disciplined is important, but blindly pushing through losses isn't automatically a virtue. Whenever I commit a wager on Moon, I try to remember that persistence alone doesn't improve the odds. Reviewing actual results and knowing when to stop are equally important skills.
